1
令狐楚，字殼士，自言國初十八學士德棻之裔。 祖崇亮，綿州昌明縣令。 父承簡，太原府功曹。 家世儒素。 楚兒童時已學屬文，弱冠應進士，貞元七年登第。 桂管觀察使王拱愛其才，欲以禮辟召，懼楚不從，乃先聞奏而後致聘。 楚以父掾太原，有庭闈之戀，又感拱厚意，登第後徑往桂林謝拱。 不預宴遊，乞歸奉養，即還太原，人皆義之。
Linghu Chu, styled Qiaoshi, claimed to be descended from Defen, one of the Eighteen Scholars of the early dynasty. His grandfather Chongliang served as magistrate of Changming County in Mian Prefecture. His father Chengjian served as a merit clerk in the Taiyuan prefectural office. His family had been devoted to Confucian learning for generations. Chu had studied literary composition since childhood. In his youth he took the jinshi examination and passed in the seventh year of the Zhenyuan era. Guiguan Observation Commissioner Wang Gong admired his talent and wished to summon him with ceremony, but feared Chu would refuse; he therefore first reported to the throne and then sent the invitation. Because his father served as a clerk in Taiyuan, Chu longed to remain near home; moved by Gong's generous regard, after passing the examination he went straight to Guilin to thank him. He declined banquets and excursions, begged leave to return and care for his parents, and went back to Taiyuan; all admired his conduct.
2
李說、嚴綬、鄭儋相繼鎮太原，高其行義，皆辟為從事。 自掌書記至節度判官，歷殿中侍御史。 楚才思俊麗。 德宗好文，每太原奏至，能辨楚之所為，頗稱之。 鄭儋在鎮暴卒，不及處分後事，軍中喧嘩，將有急變。 中夜十數騎持刃迫楚至軍門，諸將環之，令草遺表。 楚在白刃之中，搦管即成，讀示三軍，無不感泣，軍情乃安。 自是聲名益重。
Li Shuo, Yan Shou, and Zheng Dan, who successively governed Taiyuan, admired his character and all recruited him as an aide. He rose from chief secretary to military commission judge and served as Attending Censor in the Palace. Chu's literary talent was outstanding and elegant. Emperor Dezong loved literature. Whenever memorials arrived from Taiyuan, he could tell which were written by Chu and praised him highly. Zheng Dan died suddenly while in command, before later arrangements could be made. The army clamored and a sudden crisis was imminent. In the middle of the night a dozen horsemen with drawn blades forced Chu to the army gate. The generals surrounded him and ordered him to draft a final memorial. Amid naked blades, Chu took up the brush and finished at once. When it was read to the whole army, all wept, and the army's mood was settled. From this his reputation grew still greater.
3
丁父憂，以孝聞。 免喪，徵拜右拾遺，改太常博士、禮部員外郎。 母憂去官。 服闋，以刑部員外郎征，轉職方員外郎、知制誥。 楚與皇甫鎛、蕭俛同年登進士第。 元和九年，鎛初以財賦得幸，薦俛、楚俱入翰林，充學士，遷職方郎中、中書舍人，皆居內職。 時用兵淮西，言事者以師久無功，宜宥賊罷兵，唯裴度與憲宗誌在殄寇。 十二年夏，度自宰相兼彰義軍節度、淮西招撫宣慰處置使。
When his father died he observed mourning and was known for filial piety. After mourning ended he was summoned as Right Reminder, then appointed Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices and Vice Director in the Ministry of Rites. When his mother died he left office. When mourning ended he was summoned as Vice Director in the Ministry of Justice, then transferred to Vice Director in the Bureau of Appointments and appointed Drafter of Imperial Edicts. Chu, Huangfu Bo, and Xiaomian passed the jinshi examination in the same year. In the ninth year of Yuanhe, when Bo first won favor through fiscal administration, he recommended Xiaomian and Chu for the Hanlin Academy as Academicians. Chu was promoted to Director in the Bureau of Appointments and Palace Secretary, all holding inner-court posts. At that time troops were being used in Huaixi. Policy advisers held that the campaign had long been unsuccessful and the rebels should be pardoned and the army withdrawn; only Pei Du and Emperor Xianzong were determined to destroy the enemy. In summer of the twelfth year, Du left the chancellorship to serve concurrently as military commissioner of Zhangyi Army and Pacification, Comfort, and Disposition Commissioner for Huaixi.
4
宰相李逢吉與度不協，與楚相善。 楚草度淮西招撫使制，不合度旨，度請改制內三數句語。 憲宗方責度用兵，乃罷逢吉相任，亦罷楚內職，守中書舍人。 元和十三年四月，出為華州刺史。 其年十月，皇甫鎛作相，其月以楚為河陽懷節度使。 十四年四月，裴度出鎮太原。 七月，皇甫鎛薦楚入朝，自朝議郎授朝議大夫、中書侍郎、同平章事，與鎛同處臺衡，深承顧待。 十五年正月，憲宗崩，詔楚為山陵使，仍撰哀冊文。
Chancellor Li Fengji was at odds with Du and was on good terms with Chu. Chu drafted the edict appointing Du Pacification Commissioner for Huaixi, which did not accord with Du's intent. Du requested that several phrases in the edict be revised. The emperor was then reproaching Du for his use of troops. He dismissed Fengji from the chancellorship and also removed Chu from his inner-court post, leaving him as Palace Secretary. In the fourth month of the thirteenth year of Yuanhe he was appointed prefect of Hua Prefecture. In the tenth month of that year Huangfu Bo became chancellor, and in that month Chu was made military commissioner of Heyang-Huai. In the fourth month of the fourteenth year Pei Du went out to govern Taiyuan. In the seventh month Huangfu Bo recommended Chu to enter court. From Court Gentleman for Consultation he was appointed Court Gentleman for Discussion, Vice Director of the Secretariat, and Associate Councilor of State, sharing the chancellorship with Bo and deeply enjoying imperial favor. In the first month of the fifteenth year Emperor Xianzong died. An edict appointed Chu Director of the Imperial Mausoleum and ordered him to compose the lamentation text.
5
時天下怒皇甫鎛之奸邪。 穆宗即位之四日，群臣素服，班於月華門外，宣詔貶鎛，將殺之。 會蕭俛作相，托中官救解，方貶崖州。 物議以楚因鎛作相而逐裴度，群情共怒。 以蕭俛之故，無敢措言。 其年六月，山陵畢，會有告楚親吏贓汙事發，出為宣歙觀察使。 楚充奉山陵時，親吏韋正牧、奉天令于翬、翰林陰陽官等同隱官錢，不給工徒價錢，移為羨餘十五萬貫上獻。 怨訴盈路，正牧等下獄伏罪，皆誅。
At that time the whole realm was angry at Huangfu Bo's treachery and wickedness. On the fourth day after Emperor Muzong's accession, officials in plain dress lined up outside the Moon Glory Gate. An edict was proclaimed demoting Bo, and he was about to be executed. Xiaomian then became chancellor and, through inner-court eunuchs, pleaded for his release. Bo was finally demoted to Yazhou. Public opinion held that Chu had become chancellor through Bo and had driven out Pei Du; all were angry together. Because of Xiaomian, none dared speak out. In the sixth month of that year, when the mausoleum work was finished, a report emerged that Chu's close clerks had committed corruption. He was sent out as Observation Commissioner of Xuanchen. While Chu was supervising the mausoleum, his close clerks Wei Zhengmu, Fengtian magistrate Yu Hui, and Hanlin Academy yin-yang officials together concealed official funds, failed to pay laborers, and transferred a surplus of 150,000 strings of cash upward as tribute. Complaints filled the roads. Zhengmu and the others were imprisoned, convicted, and all executed.
6
楚再貶衡州刺史。 時元稹初得幸，為學士，素惡楚與鎛膠固希寵，稹草楚衡州制，略曰：「楚早以文藝，得踐班資，憲宗念才，擢居禁近。 異端斯害，獨見不明，密隳討伐之謀，潛附奸邪之黨。 因緣得地，進取多門，遂忝臺階，實妨賢路。」 楚深恨稹。 長慶元年四月，量移郢州刺史，遷太子賓客，分司東都。 二年十一月，授陜州大都督府長史、兼御史大夫、陜虢觀察使。 制下旬日，諫官論奏，言楚所犯非輕，未合居廉察之任。
Chu was demoted again to prefect of Heng Prefecture. At that time Yuan Zhen had just won favor and was an Academician. He had long hated Chu and Bo for clinging together in hope of favor. Zhen drafted Chu's Heng Prefecture appointment edict, which in summary said: "Chu early won office rank through literary accomplishment. Emperor Xianzong, mindful of his talent, promoted him to close attendance. Heterodox influences harmed him. He alone lacked clear judgment, secretly undermined plans for punitive campaigns, and secretly attached himself to wicked and treacherous factions. By connections he gained position and advanced through many doors, then disgraced the steps of the terrace and truly obstructed the path of the worthy." Chu deeply resented Zhen. In the fourth month of the first year of Changqing he was transferred to prefect of E Prefecture, then appointed Grand Mentor of the Heir Apparent and assigned to the Eastern Capital as titular official. In the eleventh month of the second year he was appointed Chief Administrator of the Metropolitan Prefecture of Shan, concurrently Censor-in-Chief, and Observation Commissioner of Shan-Guo. Ten days after the edict was issued, remonstrating officials submitted memorials saying Chu's offenses were not light and he was unfit for a surveillance and investigation post.
7
上知之，遽令追制。 時楚已至陜州，視事一日矣。 復授賓客，歸東都。 時年逢吉作相，極力援楚，以李紳在禁密沮之，未能擅柄。 敬宗即位，逢吉逐李紳，尋用楚為河南尹、兼御史大夫。 其年九月，檢校禮部尚書、汴州刺史、宣武軍節度、汴宋亳觀察等使。 汴軍素驕，累逐主帥； 前後韓弘兄弟，率以峻法繩之，人皆偷生，未能革誌。
The emperor learned of it and hastily ordered the edict recalled. By then Chu had already reached Shan Prefecture and had administered affairs for one day. He was again appointed Grand Mentor and returned to the Eastern Capital. At that time Fengji was chancellor and strongly supported Chu, but Li Shen in the inner court obstructed him and he could not monopolize power. When Emperor Jingzong acceded, Fengji drove out Li Shen and soon appointed Chu Metropolitan Governor of Henan and concurrently Censor-in-Chief. In the ninth month of that year he was made Acting Minister of Rites, prefect of Bian, military commissioner of Xuanwu Army, and observation commissioner of Bian-Song-Bo. The Bian army had long been arrogant and repeatedly drove out their commanders; the former commanders, the brothers Han Hong, generally restrained them with harsh law. The men merely eked out existence and their will could not be changed.
8
楚長於撫理，前鎮河陽，代烏重胤移鎮滄州，以河陽軍三千人為牙卒，卒咸不願從，中路叛歸，又不敢歸州，聚於境上。 楚初赴任，聞之，乃疾驅赴懷州，潰卒亦至，楚單騎喻之，咸令橐弓解甲，用為前驅，卒不敢亂。 及蒞汴州，解其酷法，以仁惠為治，去其太甚，軍民咸悅，翕然從化，後竟為善地。 汴帥前例，始至率以錢二百萬實其私藏，楚獨不取，以其羨財治廨舍數百間。 太和二年九月，徵為戶部尚書。 三年三月，檢校兵部尚書、東都留守、東畿汝都防禦使。 其年十一月，進位檢校右僕射、鄆州刺史、天平軍節度、鄆曹濮觀察等使。 奏故東平縣為天平縣。
Chu excelled at soothing administration. When he had earlier governed Heyang, Wu Chongyin was transferred from Heyang to govern Cang Prefecture. Three thousand Heyang troops were made his personal guard, but the soldiers were unwilling to follow. Midway they rebelled and returned, yet dared not return to the prefecture and gathered on the border. When Chu first took up his post and heard of it, he galloped swiftly to Huai Prefecture. The scattered soldiers also arrived. Chu went alone on horseback to instruct them, ordered them all to sheath bows and lay aside armor, and used them as vanguard. The soldiers dared not cause disorder. When he arrived at Bian Prefecture he abolished harsh laws and governed with benevolence and kindness, removing excesses. Soldiers and people alike were pleased, united in submission, and it later became a good region. By former precedent, when a Bian commander first arrived he generally deposited two million cash in his private store. Chu alone did not take it and used the surplus funds to repair several hundred government buildings. In the ninth month of the second year of Taihe he was summoned as Minister of Revenue. In the third month of the third year he was made Acting Minister of War, Eastern Capital Garrison Commander, and Defense Commissioner of the Eastern Capital and Ru Prefecture. In the eleventh month of that year he was promoted to Acting Right Vice Director of the Department of State, prefect of Yan, military commissioner of Tianping Army, and observation commissioner of Yan-Cao-Pu. He memorialized that the former Dongping County be made Tianping County.
9
屬歲旱儉，人至相食，楚均富贍貧，而無流亡者。 六年二月，改太原尹、北都留守、河東節度等使。 楚久在并州，練其風俗，因人所利而利之，雖屬歲旱，人無轉徙。 楚始自書生，隨計成名，皆在太原，實如故裏。 及是垂旄作鎮，邑老歡迎。 楚綏撫有方，軍民胥悅。 七年六月，入為吏部尚書，仍檢校右僕射。 故事，檢校高官者，便從其班。
When drought and famine struck that year and people came to eat one another, Chu equalized the rich to support the poor and there were no displaced persons. In the second month of the sixth year he was changed to Metropolitan Governor of Taiyuan, Northern Capital Garrison Commander, and military commissioner of Hedong. Chu had long been in Bingzhou and was versed in its customs. He benefited people through what they themselves found beneficial, and even in years of drought the people did not migrate. Chu had begun as a scholar. Through the examination he achieved fame, and all was in Taiyuan—it was truly like his old home. When he now governed with white hair hanging down, the elders of the district welcomed him joyfully. Chu soothed and governed with proper method; soldiers and people alike were pleased. In the sixth month of the seventh year he entered court as Minister of Personnel, still Acting Right Vice Director of the Department of State. By precedent, those holding acting high offices followed their acting rank in court order.
10
楚以正官三品不宜從二品之列，請從本班，優詔嘉之。 九年六月，轉太常卿。 十月，守尚書左僕射，進封彭陽郡開國公。 十一月，李訓兆亂，京師大擾。 訓亂之夜，文宗召右僕射鄭覃與楚宿於禁中，商量制敕，上皆欲用為宰相。 楚以王涯、賈餗冤死，敘其罪狀浮泛，仇士良等不悅，故輔弼之命移於李石。 乃以本官領鹽鐵轉運等使。 先是，鄭註上封置榷茶使額，鹽鐵使兼領之，楚奏罷之，曰：
Chu held that a regular third-rank official should not stand in second-rank order and requested to stand in his regular rank. An edict of praise approved this. In the sixth month of the ninth year he was transferred to Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices. In the tenth month he served as Left Vice Director of the Department of State and was advanced to Duke of Pengyang. In the eleventh month Li Xun plotted rebellion and the capital was greatly disturbed. On the night of Xun's rebellion, Emperor Wenzong summoned Right Vice Director Zheng Tan and Chu to stay in the inner palace to discuss edicts. The emperor wished to use both as chancellors. Chu held that Wang Ya and Jia Su had died unjustly and that the account of their crimes was vague and superficial. Qiu Shiliang and others were displeased, and so the appointment to the chancellorship shifted to Li Shi. He then held his regular office and concurrently headed the Salt and Iron Transport Commission. Earlier, Zheng Zhu had submitted a sealed memorial to establish a tea monopoly commissioner quota, which the salt commissioner concurrently held. Chu memorialized to abolish it, saying:
11
前月二十一日，內殿奏對之次，鄭覃與臣同陳論訖。 伏望聖慈早賜處分，一依舊法，不用新條。 唯納榷之時，須節級加價，商人轉賣，必校稍貴，即是錢出萬國，利歸有司。 既不害茶商，又不擾茶戶，上以彰陛下愛人之德，下以竭微臣憂國之心。 遠近傳聞，必當感悅。 從之。 先是，元和十年，出內庫弓箭陌刀賜左右街使，充宰相入朝以為翼衛，及建福門而止。 至是，因訓、註之亂，悉罷之。
On the twenty-first day of last month, during an audience in the inner hall, Zheng Tan and I together finished presenting our views. I humbly hope Your Sacred Kindness will soon grant disposition and follow the old law entirely, not using the new regulations. Only when collecting the monopoly levy should prices be raised by stages. When merchants resell, prices must be somewhat higher—thus money comes from all lands and profit returns to the authorities. This neither harms tea merchants nor disturbs tea households. Above it manifests Your Majesty's virtue of loving the people; below it exhausts this humble minister's heart of concern for the state. When the report spreads far and near, all will surely be moved and pleased. The emperor approved. Earlier, in the tenth year of Yuanhe, bows, arrows, and broadswords from the inner storehouse were issued to the left and right street commissioners. Chancellors entering court used them as escort guards, stopping at the Jianfu Gate. Now, because of the rebellion of Xun and Zhu, all were abolished.
12
楚又奏：「諸道新授方鎮節度使等，具帑抹，帶器仗，就尚書省兵部參辭。 伏以軍國異容，古今定制，若不由舊，斯為改常。 未聞省閣之門，忽內弓刀之器。 鄭註外蒙恩寵，內蓄兇狂，首創奸謀，將興亂兆。 致王璠、郭行余之輩，敢驅將吏，直詣闕庭。 震驚乘輿，騷動京國，血濺朝路，屍僵禁街。 史冊所書，人神共憤，既往不咎，其源尚開。 前件事宜，伏乞速令停罷，如須參謝，即具公服。」
Chu also memorialized: "Newly appointed military commissioners of the various circuits and the like should bring traveling funds and weapons and present themselves for audience at the Ministry of War in the Department of State. I humbly consider that military and civil attire differ and ancient and modern regulations are fixed. If the old way is not followed, this is to change what is constant. I have never heard of bow-and-blade weapons suddenly inside the gates of the Secretariat. Zheng Zhu outwardly received imperial favor yet inwardly harbored fierce wickedness. He first devised treacherous plots and was about to raise the omen of disorder. He caused men like Wang Fan and Guo Xingyu to dare drive generals and clerks straight to the palace gates. The imperial carriage was shaken and the capital disturbed. Blood splashed on the road to court and corpses lay stiff in the forbidden streets. What histories record, men and spirits alike resent. Though the past is not blamed, the source remains open. Regarding the former matter, I humbly beg that it be swiftly ordered stopped. If audience is required, let them wear only official robes."
13
從之。 又奏請罷修曲江亭絹一萬三千七百匹，回修尚書省，從之。 開成元年上巳，賜百僚曲江亭宴。 楚以新誅大臣，不宜賞宴，獨稱疾不赴，論者美之。 以權在內官，累上疏乞解使務。 其年四月，檢校左僕射、興元尹，充山南西道節度使。 二年十一月，卒於鎮，年七十二，冊贈司空，謚曰文。 楚風儀嚴重，若不可犯；
The emperor approved. He also memorialized requesting abolition of the 13,700 bolts of silk for repairing Qujiang Pavilion and their reallocation to repair the Department of State. The emperor approved. On the third day of the third month in the first year of Kaicheng, the emperor bestowed a banquet at Qujiang Pavilion on the hundred officials. Chu held that since great ministers had just been executed, it was improper to reward them with a banquet. He alone pleaded illness and did not attend, and commentators praised him. Because power lay with inner-court eunuchs, he repeatedly submitted memorials begging to be relieved of commission duties. In the fourth month of that year he was made Acting Left Vice Director of the Department of State and Metropolitan Governor of Xingyuan, military commissioner of Shannan West Circuit. In the eleventh month of the second year he died in his post at age seventy-two. He was posthumously enfeoffed as Minister of Works and given the posthumous title Wen. Chu's bearing was stern and grave, as if he could not be violated;
14
然寬厚有禮，門無雜賓。 嘗與從事宴語方酣，有非類偶至，立命徹席，毅然色變。 累居重任，貞操如初。 未終前三日，猶吟詠自若。 疾甚，諸子進藥，未賞入口，曰：「修短之期，分以定矣，何須此物？」 前一日，召從事李商隱曰：「吾氣魄已殫，情思俱盡，然所懷未已，強欲自寫聞天，恐辭語乖舛，子當助我成之。」 即秉筆自書曰： 書訖，謂其子緒、綯曰：「吾生無益於人，勿請謚號。
yet he was generous and courteous, and no improper guests entered his gate. Once while drinking and conversing with aides he was in high spirits. When someone unfitting arrived by chance, he immediately ordered the feast withdrawn and his expression turned stern. Though he repeatedly held heavy responsibility, his integrity remained as at first. Three days before his end he still chanted and composed as usual. When his illness was severe his sons brought medicine. Before it entered his mouth he said: "The term of life long or short is already fixed by fate—why need this thing?" The day before, he summoned his aide Li Shangyin and said: "My vital breath is already exhausted and my feelings and thoughts are all spent, yet what I still carry has not ended. I force myself to write and inform Heaven, but fear my words may be mistaken—you must help me complete it." He then took up the brush and wrote himself: When the writing was finished he told his sons Xu and Tao: "In life I was of no benefit to others—do not request a posthumous title.
15
葬日，勿請鼓吹，唯以布車一乘，余勿加飾。 銘誌但誌宗門，秉筆者無擇高位。」 當歿之夕，有大星隕於寢室之上，其光燭廷。 楚端坐與家人告訣，言已而終。 嗣子奉行遺旨。 詔曰：「生為名臣，歿有理命。 終始之分，可謂兩全。 鹵簿哀榮之末節，難違往意；
On the day of burial do not request ceremonial music. Use only one cloth carriage and add no further ornament. The inscription should record only the clan. Let the writer not be chosen for high rank." On the night of his death a great star fell above his sleeping chamber and its light illuminated the courtyard. Chu sat upright and took leave of his family. When he finished speaking he died. His heir carried out his final instructions. An edict said: "In life he was a famed minister; in death he had a rational fate. The division of beginning and end may be called fully complete. The final rites of escort and glory are minor matters and hard to violate his former intent;
16

The Lamentation Text for Emperor Xianzong that he composed was rich and solemn in literary feeling and was valued by writers. Chu's younger brother Ding, styled Luchang. When he died he was posthumously made Minister of Rites. Xu received office by hereditary privilege and served successively as prefect of Sui, Shou, and Ru prefectures. While in Ru Prefecture he had able administration, and the people of the prefecture requested an inscribed stele praising his virtue. Because his younger brother Can was in the chancellorship, Xu submitted a memorial saying: "My late father in the Yuanhe era specially received imperial favor. My younger brother Tao's office did not come through others but issued from the imperial heart. Your servant has seen the edict that because I governed Ru Prefecture and roughly established administrative merit, officials and people sought to erect a stele of praise. I beg that this be recalled and stopped. When I governed Sui Prefecture the people begged me to remain and I received top and bottom ratings in assessment. When I was transferred to Vice Governor of Henan I was given gold and purple. This fame is already known below the sun; there is no need to erect another stele of praise. In the fourth year he was transferred to Vice Minister of Revenue and directed the ministry's affairs. In the thirteenth year he was dismissed from the chancellorship and made Acting Minister of Works, Associate Councilor of State, Metropolitan Governor of Hezhong, and military commissioner of Hezhong-Jin-Jiang. In the second year of Xiantong he was changed to prefect of Bian and military commissioner of Xuanwu Army. Chief Military Escort Li Xiang told Tao: "The Xu troops returned without authorization—they surely have no good intent.

雖無詔命除討，權變制在籓方。 昨其黨來投，言其數不逾二千，而虛張舟航旗幟，恐人見其實。 涉境已來，心頗憂惴。 計其水路，須出高郵縣界，河岸鬥峻而水深狹。 若出奇兵邀之，俾荻船縱火於前，勁兵奮擊於後，敗走必矣。 若不於此誅鋤，俟濟淮、泗，合徐人負怨之徒，不下十萬，則禍亂非細也。」 綯性懦緩，又以不奉詔命，謂湘曰：「長淮已南，他不為暴。 從他過去，余非吾事也。」
Though there is no edict ordering suppression, expedient authority to act lies with the frontier governor. Yesterday their party came to surrender and said their number did not exceed two thousand, yet they falsely displayed boats, banners, and flags, fearing people would see their true strength. Since they crossed the border I have been quite anxious. Considering their water route, they must pass the border of Gaoyou County, where the river bank is steep and the water deep and narrow. If surprise troops are sent to intercept them, set fire to reed boats ahead and strike fiercely from behind, they will surely flee in defeat. If they are not destroyed here, when they cross the Huai and Si and join Xu people bearing grievances, they will number no less than one hundred thousand—then calamity and disorder will be no small matter." Tao was by nature timid and slow, and because he had no imperial edict he told Xiang: "South of the Long Huai they will not commit violence. Let them pass by—the rest is not my affair."

其年冬，龐勛殺崔彥曾，據徐州，聚眾六七萬。 徐無兵食，乃分遣賊帥攻剽淮南諸郡，滁、和、楚、壽繼陷。 谷食既盡，淮南之民多為賊所啖。 時兩淮郡縣多陷，唯杜慆守泗州，賊攻之經年，不能下。 初，詔綯為徐州南面招討使。 賊攻泗州急，綯令李湘將兵五千人援之。 賊聞湘來援，遣人致書於綯，辭情遜順，言：「朝廷累有詔赦宥，但抗拒者三兩人耳，旦夕圖去之，即束身請命，願相公保任之。」 綯即奏聞，請賜勛節鉞，仍誡李湘但戍淮口，賊已招降，不得立異。
That winter Pang Xun killed Cui Yanzeng, seized Xu Prefecture, and gathered a host of sixty or seventy thousand. Xu had no troops or grain, so they sent bandit chiefs to raid the prefectures of Huainan. Chu, He, Chu, and Shou fell in succession. When grain was exhausted, many people of Huainan were eaten by the bandits. At that time many prefectures and counties of the two Huai regions had fallen. Only Du Tao held Si Prefecture, and though the bandits attacked for a year they could not take it. Initially an edict appointed Tao Pacification Commissioner south of Xu Prefecture. When the bandits pressed the attack on Si Prefecture, Tao ordered Li Xiang to lead five thousand troops to aid it. When the bandits heard Xiang was coming to aid, they sent a man with a letter to Tao, humble and compliant in tone, saying: "The court has repeatedly issued edicts of pardon. Only two or three men resist. We plan to remove them before long, then bind ourselves and beg for orders—we hope the Lord Chancellor will vouch for us." Tao immediately reported to the throne and requested that Xun be granted the staff of command. He also warned Li Xiang only to garrison the Huai mouth—the bandits had already surrendered and he must not act differently.

由是湘軍解甲安寢，去警徹備，日與賊軍相對，歡笑交言。 一日，賊軍乘間，步騎徑入湘壘，淮卒五千人皆被生縶送徐州，為賊蒸而食之。 湘與監軍郭厚本為龐勛斷手足，以徇於康承訓軍。 時浙西杜審權發軍千人，與李湘約會兵，大將翟行約勇敢知名。 浙軍未至而湘軍敗。 賊乃分兵，立淮南旗幟，為交鬥之狀。 行約軍望見，急趨之，千人並為賊所縛。 送徐州。
Because of this Xiang's army laid aside armor and slept peacefully, relaxed vigilance and defenses, and daily faced the bandit army laughing and conversing. One day the bandit army seized an opening. Infantry and cavalry entered Xiang's camp directly, and all five thousand Huai soldiers were captured alive and sent to Xu Prefecture to be steamed and eaten by the bandits. Xiang and Military Commissioner Guo Houben had their hands and feet cut off by Pang Xun and were displayed before Kang Chengxun's army. At that time Zhexi's Du Shenquan sent one thousand troops to join Xiang in combined operations. The great general Zhai Xingyue was brave and famous. The Zhe army had not yet arrived when Xiang's army was defeated. The bandits then divided their forces, raised Huainan banners, and made a show of mutual combat. Xingyue's army saw them and hurried toward them. All one thousand were bound by the bandits. They were sent to Xu Prefecture.

Since Tao had lost his army, the court sent Left Guard General Ma Ju, Southwest Pacification Commissioner for Xu Prefecture, to replace Tao as military commissioner of Huainan. In the eighth month of the twelfth year he was appointed Acting Minister of Works and Grand Mentor of the Heir Apparent, assigned to the Eastern Capital as titular official. In the thirteenth year, with his regular office he became Metropolitan Governor of Fengxiang and military commissioner of Fengxiang-Long, advanced to Duke of Zhao with a fief of three thousand households, and died. His sons were Hao, Huan, and Fen. Hao, while young, took the jinshi examination but stopped because his father held an inner-court post. When Tao assisted in government for ten years, Hao, through kinship with Zheng Hao, was arrogant and lawless, daily given to feasting and pleasure, and bribes filled his gate. Inside and outside all watched him sidelong. Because Tao's factional support was then flourishing, none dared speak. When Emperor Yizong acceded, complainants were not few, and so Tao was dismissed from the axis of power.

Then receiving generous favor I disgraced the pivot of power. The matter was improper, so I ordered him to stop the examination and it should have ended—nineteen years in all. Among them were Zheng Yi, grandson of former Minister of Revenue Huan; Pei Hongyu, son of former Chancellor Xiu; Wei Tao, son of former Chancellor Fu; and Hao—all sons of famed ministers, said to lack real talent. Remonstrance Official Cui Xuan submitted a memorial criticizing this, saying: "Linghu Hao yesterday, because his father held the chancellorship, had power in one gate. Those who sought favors flocked like wind to a clique; those who acted rashly gathered like clouds of the wicked. Each year when candidates passed the examination gate and the pure ranks of court received office, though the matter seemed to come from Tao, selection lay entirely with Hao. The clamor was like a market, as if no one else existed. His power moved within the realm and his momentum overturned the world. On the day Tao left the chancellorship to govern a frontier post he had Hao submit his examination papers. How can the father be at the pivot of power yet alone twist the literary handle? I beg that the Censorate be ordered to investigate according to the dates of the examination papers."

Hao was condemned by all and his official reputation did not prosper. Huan and Fen both passed the jinshi examination. Huan reached Palace Secretary. Ding's son Jian; Jian's sons Cheng and Xiang. Cheng also passed the jinshi examination and was repeatedly recruited to commissioner staffs. Niu Sengru, styled Si'an, was a descendant of Duke Qizhang Niu Hong, Minister of Works of the Sui. His grandfather was Shao.

父幼簡，官卑。 僧孺進士擢第，登賢良方正制科，釋褐伊闕尉，遷監察御史，轉殿中，歷禮部員外郎。 元和中，改都官，知臺雜，尋換考功員外郎，充集賢直學士。 穆宗即位，以庫部郎中知制誥。 其年十一月，改御史中丞。 以州府刑獄淹滯，人多冤抑，僧孺條疏奏請，按劾相繼，中外肅然。 長慶元年，宿州刺史李直臣坐贓當死，直臣賂中貴人為之申理，僧孺堅執不回。 穆宗面喻之曰：「直臣事雖僭失，然此人有經度才，可委之邊任，朕欲貸其法。」

Sengru was selected through the jinshi examination, passed the Exceptionally Qualified and Upright recruitment, left office as warden of Yique, was promoted to Investigating Censor, transferred to the Palace, and served as Vice Director in the Ministry of Rites. In the Yuanhe era he was changed to the Bureau of Punishments, directed palace censorial affairs, soon changed to Vice Director in the Bureau of Evaluations, and served as Academician of the Hall of Assembled Worthies. When Emperor Muzong acceded he became Director in the Treasuries Ministry and Drafter of Imperial Edicts. In the eleventh month of that year he was changed to Vice Censor-in-Chief. Because prefectural prisons delayed cases and many people suffered wrongful oppression, Sengru submitted detailed memorials requesting investigation and impeachment in succession. Inside and outside grew stern. In the first year of Changqing, Su Prefecture magistrate Li Zhichen was convicted of corruption and should die. Zhichen bribed inner-court favorites to plead his case, but Sengru firmly held and did not yield. Emperor Muzong instructed him face to face: "Zhichen's matter, though excessive and wrongful, yet this man has talent for planning and may be entrusted with frontier duty. I wish to pardon him by law."

Sengru replied: "Ordinary men without talent merely hold salary and seek favor. The emperor establishes law to bind treacherous heroes precisely because talent is abundant. An Lushan and Zhu Ci exceeded others in talent yet troubled and disordered the realm. How much more Zhichen's small talent—why bend the law?" The emperor praised his upholding of law and personally bestowed gold and purple. In the first month of the second year he was appointed Vice Minister of Revenue. In the third month of the third year, with his regular office he became Associate Councilor of State. Earlier, when Han Hong entered court, because of old Xuanwu affairs many spread rumors. His son Gongwu used family wealth to bribe the powerful and many speakers, and among the ranks all received his gifts. Soon father and son both died. The orphaned grandson was young. Jiangxia city's soil was loose and bad and hard to build walls. Every year additional plank construction was added and a levy of green thatch imposed for covering. Within five years all walls were tiled and repaired and the corruption was permanently removed. He followed the emperor returning to the capital. When he reached Chencang his illness was severe and only after a year did he recover. Chancellor Zhang Jun as Pacification Commissioner memorialized Hui as judge and Acting Left Regular Cavalryman. When the edict reached Fengxiang he was urged to hurry to court. Hui told those close to him: "The state's step is now difficult and the imperial residence has just been restored. The treasury is all empty and we truly rely on all ministers to cooperate and join hearts with the royal house. Muzong asked the chancellors: "Is there a method that must win in using troops?" Mian replied: "Arms are baleful instruments and battle is a perilous affair. In ancient use of arms one did not cut off sacrifices, did not kill the wounded, did not capture the gray-haired, and did not violate standing grain. To pacify the people and forbid violence is the highest of armies. It is like rescue more urgent than fire and water. Therefore the king's army has campaigns but no battles—this is the way that must win. In the fourth year he was made Acting Minister of Revenue, prefect of Yan, and military commissioner of Yan-Yi-Hai. He again entered court as Grand Mentor of the Heir Apparent.

倣上疏論之曰： 伏睹陛下留神天竺，屬意桑門，內設道場，中開講會，或手錄梵策，或口揚佛音。 雖時啟於延英，從容四輔； 慮稍稀於聽政，廢失萬機。 居安思危，不可忽也。 夫從容者，君也，必疇咨於臣，盡忠匡救，外逆其耳，內沃其心； 陳臯陶之謨，述仲虺之誥； 發揮王道，恢益帝圖，非賜對之間，徒侍坐而已。
He also repeatedly visited various temples and gave offerings beyond measure. Fang submitted a memorial criticizing this, saying: I observe that Your Majesty fixes attention on India and turns intent to the sangha, establishing dharma halls within and opening lecture assemblies in the middle, sometimes personally copying Sanskrit texts or orally expounding Buddhist sounds. Though at times this opens at Yanying with the four assistants at ease; I fear audience of government grows somewhat rare and the myriad affairs are neglected and lost. In security think of peril—this cannot be slighted. Ease belongs to the ruler, who must consult ministers, exhaust loyalty and rescue, outwardly oppose the ear and inwardly irrigate the heart; set forth the counsels of Gao Yao and narrate the admonitions of Zhong Hui;

In former years Han Yu already offended Emperor Xianzong; today this humble minister is gladly willing to accept distant banishment. When the memorial was submitted the emperor greatly approved. In the fourth year with his regular office he acted as chief examiner, was transferred to Vice Minister of Rites, then Minister of Revenue. As Acting Minister of Works he was sent out as governor of Hua Prefecture, military commissioner of the Yicheng Army, and Commissioner of Defense and Disposition of Zheng, Hua, and Ying. Inner-court officials grasped troops and the royal house was muddied and disordered. Fang's spirit was forceful and his discourse straight; colleagues envied him. He left governance of affairs and was sent out as governor of Guang Prefecture and military commissioner of Lingnan. Fang was public-minded and incorrupt. Li Shi, whose courtesy name was Zhongyu, was a man of Longxi. His grandfather was Jian; his father Ming. Shi passed the jinshi examination and followed Duke of Liang Li Ting through four commands as aide. Shi was clever in debate and had stratagems, especially skilled in clerkly arts—the frontier staffs praised him. From Ting's campaigns he always managed remaining commission affairs; nothing was left undone. In the third year of Taihe he was Marching Army Marshal of Zheng Prefecture. At the time Ting held troops in Hebei and ordered Shi to enter court to report. His answers were clear and eloquent and Wenzong looked on him with approval. When the staff was dismissed he entered court as Director in the Ministry of Works, directing salt and iron cases.

In the tenth month he was transferred to Vice Minister of Revenue, directing Department of Revenue affairs. After the seventh year of Taihe, eminent old ministers were passed over and not used. The intent was to promote and use newly advanced isolated men, hoping thereby to have no factions and reform former abuses—therefore Jia Su and Shu Yuanyu suddenly rose to great employment. The Jiangxi and Hunan observation commissioners, because of the recent Xun and Zhu turmoil in which many clerks and soldiers died, presented one hundred twenty portions of official soldiers' clothing and grain to recruit followers for the chancellors. Shi memorialized: "Chancellors above assist sacred government and below govern all offices. Shi memorialized: "Your servant employed Yi because he understood money and grain—I did not expect such greed and baseness!" The emperor said: "The chancellor only employs those he knows; when there is fault then punish. Those you employ and do not cover their wickedness—this may be called utmost fairness. Former chancellors employing men, when there was fault curved to hide it, not wishing people to impeach—this is greatly wrong. Only know ability then raise; raise without losing office then reward—naturally easy to get the right men. Why must one conceal?" On the fifth day of the first month of the third year Shi from Qinren Lane was about to enter court at dawn. Bandits broke into the former residence of Guo the late father-in-law; pursuing with bow he was reached. The arrow only broke skin and the horse bolted and turned.
86
盜已伏坊門，揮刀斫石，斷馬尾，竟以馬逸得還私第。 上聞之駭愕，遣中使撫問，賜金瘡藥，因差六軍兵士三十人衛從宰相。 是日，京師大恐，常參官入朝者，九人而已，旬日方安。 石拜章辭位者三。 乃加金紫光祿大夫、中書侍郎、同平章事、江陵尹、荊南節度使。 李訓之亂，人情危迫，天子起石於常僚之中，付以衡柄。 石以身徇國，不顧患難，振舉朝綱，國威再復。 而中官仇士良切齒惡之，而伏戎加害。
The bandit already lay in wait at the ward gate, swung blade and struck Shi, severed the horse's tail, yet by the horse's bolt he returned to his private residence. When the emperor heard he was startled, sent an inner-court envoy to comfort and inquire, bestowed gold and wound medicine, and dispatched thirty Six Army soldiers to guard the chancellors. That day the capital was greatly afraid. Officials entering regular audience numbered only nine; only after ten days was it settled. Shi submitted memorials resigning office three times. He was then advanced to Grand Master for Splendid Happiness with Gold Seal, Vice Director of the Secretariat, Associate Councilor of State, Metropolitan Governor of Jiangling, and military commissioner of Jingnan. In Li Xun's turmoil people's hearts were perilous. The Son of Heaven raised Shi from among regular officials and entrusted him with the balance of power. Shi gave himself for the state without regard for hardship, raised court discipline, and national prestige was restored. Yet inner-court eunuch Qiu Shiliang gnashed teeth in hatred and hidden foes added harm.
87
天子深知其故，畏逼而不能理，乃至罷免。 及石赴鎮，賜宴之儀並闕，人士傷之，恥君子之道消也。 石至鎮，表讓中書侍郎，乃加檢校兵部尚書、兼平章事。 武宗即位，就加檢校尚書右僕射。 會昌三年十月，加檢校司空、平章事、隴西郡開國伯、食邑七百戶、太原尹、北都留守、河東節度觀察等使。 時澤潞劉稹阻兵，以石嘗為太原副使，諳練北門軍政，故代劉沔鎮之。 初，沔以兵三千人戍橫水。 王師之討澤潞也，王逢軍於榆社，訴兵少，請益之，詔石以太原之卒赴榆社。
The Son of Heaven deeply knew the reason yet feared coercion and could not judge—thus to dismissal. When Shi went to his post the banquet rites were all lacking. Gentlemen were wounded and ashamed that the way of the noble man was fading. When Shi reached his post he memorialized declining Vice Director of the Secretariat and was advanced to Acting Minister of War and Associate Councilor of State. When Emperor Wuzong acceded he was advanced to Acting Right Vice Director of the Department of State. In the tenth month of the third year of Huichang he was advanced to Acting Minister of Works, Councilor of State, Baron of Longxi with seven hundred households, Metropolitan Governor of Taiyuan, Northern Capital Garrison Commander, and military commissioner of Hedong. At that time Zelu Liu Zhen resisted with troops. Because Shi had once been vice commissioner of Taiyuan and was versed in Northern Gate military government, he replaced Liu Mian to govern. Initially Mian had three thousand troops garrison Hengshui. When the royal army attacked Zelu, Wang Feng's army was at Yushe and complained troops were few and begged reinforcement. An edict ordered Shi to send Taiyuan troops to Yushe.
88
石乃割橫水戍卒一千五百人，令別將楊弁率之，以赴王逢。 舊例發軍，人給二縑。 石以支計不足，量減一匹，軍人聚怨。 又將及歲除，促令上路，眾愈不悅。 楊弁乘其釁謀亂，出言激動軍人。 四年正月，軍亂逐石，朝廷乃以晉絳觀察使崔元式代還。 五年，檢校司徒、東都留守、判東都尚書省事、畿汝都防禦使。 以太子少保分司卒。
Shi then cut one thousand five hundred from the Hengshui garrison and ordered Vice General Yang Bian to lead them to join Wang Feng. By former precedent when troops were dispatched each man was given two bolts of silk. Shi because expenditure accounts were insufficient measured and reduced by one bolt. Soldiers gathered resentment. Also as year-end drew near they were urged to set out on the road. The crowd grew more displeased. Yang Bian seized the opening to plot rebellion and spoke to incite the soldiers. In the first month of the fourth year the army rebelled and drove out Shi. The court then sent Jin-Jiang Observation Commissioner Cui Yuanshi to replace and return. In the fifth year he was made Acting Minister of Works, Eastern Capital Garrison Commander, directing Eastern Capital Department of State affairs, and Defense Commissioner of Ji and Ru. He died as Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent assigned to titular duty.
89
石弟福，字能之。 太和七年登進士第，累辟使府。 石為宰相，自薦弟於延英，言福才堪理人，授監察御史。 累遷尚書郎，出為商、鄭、汝、潁四州刺史。 大中時，檢校工部尚書、滑州刺史、兼御史大夫，充義成軍節度、鄭滑潁觀察使。 入為刑部侍郎，累遷刑部、戶部尚書。 乾符初，以檢校右僕射、襄州刺史、兼御史大夫充山南東道節度。 四年，草賊王仙芝徒黨數萬寇掠山南。
Shi's younger brother Fu, styled Nengzhi. In the seventh year of Taihe he passed the jinshi examination and was repeatedly recruited to commissioner staffs. When Shi was chancellor he recommended his younger brother at Yanying, saying Fu's talent sufficed to govern people, and appointed him Investigating Censor. He was repeatedly promoted to Director in a ministry and went out as prefect of Shang, Zheng, Ru, and Ying. In the Dazhong era he was made Acting Minister of Works, prefect of Hua, concurrently Censor-in-Chief, and military commissioner of Yicheng Army and observation commissioner of Zheng-Hua-Ying. He entered court as Vice Minister of Punishments and was repeatedly promoted to Minister of Punishments and Revenue. At the beginning of Qianfu he was made Acting Right Vice Director of the Department of State, prefect of Xiang, concurrently Censor-in-Chief, and military commissioner of Shannan East Circuit. In the fourth year grass bandit Wang Xianzhi's followers numbered tens of thousands raiding Shannan.
90
福團練鄉兵，屯集要路，賊不敢犯。 其秋，賊陷嶽、鄂、饒、信等州。 十二月，逼江陵，節度使楊知溫求援於福； 福即自率州兵及沙阤五百騎赴援。 時賊已陷江陵之郛，聞福兵至，乃退去。 僖宗嘉之，就加檢校司空、同平章事。 歸朝，終於太子太傅。 史臣曰：彭陽奇章，起徒步而升臺鼎。
Fu trained local militia, gathered at strategic points, and the bandits dared not violate. That autumn the bandits seized Yue, E, Rao, and Xin prefectures. In the twelfth month they pressed Jiangling. Military Commissioner Yang Zhiwen begged aid from Fu; Fu immediately led prefectural troops and five hundred Shatuo cavalry to aid. When the bandits had already seized Jiangling's outer city and heard Fu's troops had arrived they then withdrew. Emperor Xizong approved and advanced him to Acting Minister of Works and Associate Councilor of State. Returning to court he ended as Grand Preceptor of the Heir Apparent. The historian says: Pengyang Qizhang rose from commoner to terrace and tripod.
91
觀其人文彪炳，潤色邦典，射策命中，橫絕一時，誠俊賢也。 而峨冠曳組，論道於臯、夔之伍，孰曰不然？ 如能蹈道匪躬，中立無黨，則其善盡矣。 蕭太師貞獨嫉惡，不為利回，不以夷、惠儗之，俾之經綸，則其道至矣。 開成之始，帝道方淪，石於此時欲振頹緒，幾嬰戕賊，可為咄嗟。 多僻之時，止堪太息。 贊曰：喬松孤立，蘿蔦夤緣。 柔附淩雲，豈曰能賢？
Observing his literary brilliance adorning and enriching state statutes, hitting the target in policy examinations, transcending his age—truly he was outstanding talent. Yet with high cap and trailing ribbons, discussing the Way among the ranks of Gao Yao and Kui—who would say otherwise? If he could tread the Way without self, stand neutral without faction, then his goodness would be complete. Grand Preceptor Xu was uniquely upright and detested evil, not turned by profit. Not compared to Bo Yi or Hui of Liu—entrust him with weaving the realm and then his Way would reach utmost. At the beginning of Kaicheng the imperial Way was sinking. Shi at this time wished to revive the declining thread and nearly met slaughter—a matter for exclamation. In a time of many perversities one can only sigh deeply. Softly attaching and soaring aloft—can this be called able and worthy? Softly attaching and soaring aloft—can this be called able and worthy?
92
嗚呼楚、孺，道喪曲全！ 蕭、李相才，致之外篇。
Alas Chu and Sengru—the Way lost yet wholly preserved! Xiao and Li had chancellor talent—set beyond this chapter.
